items.title: DigiCert Confirms Data Breach Exposing Customer Details and Sensitive Identity Documents
items.summary: DigiCert has confirmed a data breach involving an internal business system that stored customer contact details and identity documents. Unauthorized access exposed archived information, including names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses. A small minority of affected customer accounts also contained passports, driver’s licenses, utility bills, or other documents showing names and addresses. The company said the incident affected only a small proportion of its archived data. Its public report does not provide a total number of affected people, organizations, or documents. DigiCert confirmed the unauthorized data access on October 19, 2026, and filed its preliminary incident report the following day. DigiCert said its Certificate Authority services, CertCentral, and DigiCert ONE were unaffected. The company said customer login credentials and issued certificates remain secure. Investigators found no certificate issuance, validation changes, or revocation activity linked to the unauthorized account. Customers do not need to replace active certificates because of this incident. Troy Hunt shared DigiCert’s notification on X, asking, “Anyone else get one of these from @digicert?” The email said the company was reviewing identity documents to identify affected individuals and would notify them once the review was complete. DigiCert Confirms Data Breach The exposure began with an infrastructure migration on February 4, 2025. DigiCert moved the business system from a network segment restricted by a virtual private network, or VPN, to another availability zone. That change accidentally made the internal system accessible from the internet without a security review of its new exposure. An account registration feature, intended for other uses of the account management platform, also became available. Accounts created through that feature were not covered by the multifactor authentication required for DigiCert staff. Although these accounts had no application assigned, they received read-only access to archived information, revealing a gap in permission checks. According to DigiCert’s incident report , staff noticed non-DigiCert accounts on June 18, 2026. An initial review incorrectly concluded that accounts without an assigned application could not access data. A web application firewall blocked new registrations through the external access path, but existing access remained a concern. A report from DigiCert’s managed security research program followed on June 21. Engineers confirmed the registration issue and released an authorization fix on July 2. Investigators later established that unauthorized data access occurred between June 27 and July 2. DigiCert initially treated the problem as an account-creation issue rather than a data-access incident. The company first suspected access to archived information on October 12. Retained logs and audit records helped investigators reconstruct the access window and link activity to the account. The account could read records but could not change them, approve identity checks, or issue certificates. DigiCert subsequently disabled self-registration, moved remaining exposed endpoints behind private network infrastructure, reset business system passwords, and strengthened monitoring. It also completed a permissions review and required security approval for network access changes. The report’s action items include further checks on external exposure and account alerts. This disclosure concerns archived customer information, not compromised certificate operations. It differs from the earlier DigiCert support-system breach involving code-signing certificates and the 2024 DNS validation error that required certificate replacements. Here, the central failure was allowing newly registered accounts to read sensitive records. DigiCert’s stated lesson is direct: internal tools need explicit authorization checks, even when network restrictions are expected to protect them. items.title: DreamHost Confirms Data Breach – Hackers Stole Customer Credentials and Accessed Emails
items.summary: DreamHost has confirmed a breach that exposed customer login details after hackers exploited its web-based File Manager. The hosting provider said attackers obtained FTP/SFTP usernames and passwords, along with some webmail credentials. In a small number of cases, private mailbox contents may also have been viewed. The company discovered unauthorized access on October 23, 2026. Its investigation identified a potential exposure window stretching back to approximately August. Customers who used File Manager during that period have been told to treat their file transfer credentials as compromised, even while investigators continue checking the full impact. DreamHost currently estimates that well under approximately 10% of its hosted email and FTP/SFTP accounts were affected. That figure refers to accounts, not a confirmed number of individual customers. Some users received precautionary password reset notices but may not have had their credentials exposed. The confirmation follows DreamHost’s earlier email and FTP password resets , which initially left the cause unclear. Those resets stopped affected users from signing in until account owners created new passwords. File Manager returned online on October 26, according to the earlier incident reporting. DreamHost found no evidence that attackers accessed control panel logins or customer billing details. It also said full payment card numbers are not stored on its systems because an outside processor handles card payments. These findings remain subject to the ongoing investigation rather than proving that every possible risk has been excluded. DreamHost Confirms Data Breach In its October 29 security incident disclosure , DreamHost said the entry point was a flaw in third-party software behind File Manager. The browser-based tool lets customers manage website files. The notice does not name the software, describe the vulnerability, or provide a CVE identifier. Attackers also reached certain webmail systems and obtained credentials belonging to a limited number of users. DreamHost reset those passwords and ended active sessions on October 23. It is contacting customers individually where investigators believe mailbox contents may have been viewed. The company has not confirmed widespread email theft. Ending sessions matters alongside changing passwords. Separate reporting on stolen browser cookies and account takeovers explains how an authenticated session can expose email without another login. However, DreamHost’s public announcement does not explicitly confirm stolen session tokens, so that detail should not be treated as established by this notice. DreamHost took the affected File Manager server offline and preserved it for forensic work. It then rebuilt the service with added safeguards and monitoring, changed potentially exposed internal credentials, and brought in outside security experts. Reviews of other customer-facing tools and required regulator notifications are also underway. Affected users need their account owner to reset passwords through DreamHost’s control panel. The company recommends unique passwords, changing reused credentials elsewhere, and updating saved passwords in email and file transfer clients. Customers should inspect website files for unexpected changes and check mailbox forwarding rules and filters for unfamiliar entries. Customers should type panel.dreamhost.com directly into their browser rather than follow login links in unexpected messages. DreamHost says its incident emails never request passwords or ask recipients to sign in through a link. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: OpenAI Cyber Model Uncovers 948 Linux Kernel Privilege Escalation Vulnerabilities
items.summary: OpenAI says an automated research pipeline found and proved 948 separate Linux kernel privilege escalation flaws in one run. These bugs could let a normal local user gain root access. The run took place in mid-October 2026 and used an upcoming cyber model, as OpenAI explains in its research write-up. The system first scanned the kernel for the parts a low-privileged user can reach. These “Scout” agents picked 5,034 audit targets, about 2.8 million lines of code or roughly 7% of the kernel. “Analyst” agents then produced 2,308 candidate findings in 12 hours. A candidate is only a guess until someone proves it. Triage agents built proof-of-concept code and ran it in isolated virtual machines with the Kernel Address Sanitizer turned on. Within 30 hours, 1,724 findings (about 74.7%) were reproduced. Only 3.1% were wrong because the model assumed an impossible condition. Next, exploit agents tested the bugs on systems with common protections such as SMEP, SMAP, KASLR, and HARDENED_USERCOPY. They produced 291 information leak proofs and 1,169 working privilege escalation exploits. OpenAI Uncovers 948 Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities After variant analysis, OpenAI counted 948 unique vulnerabilities and wrote 948 patches for them. Human researchers reviewed the results before reporting. This builds on the Patch the Planet program from June, when GPT-5.5-Cyber produced 24 Linux privilege escalation exploits. Our earlier report on GPT-5.5-Cyber covers that launch. The full run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, or about $1,279 per exploit. OpenAI calls this an upper bound and expects better tooling to cut it. It compared the output with public bounties. Using $20,000 from Pwn2Own and $70,000 from TyphoonPWN , the 948 bugs would be worth $18.9 million to $66.3 million. On a hardened kernelCTF setup, the pipeline got 21 privilege escalation exploits for about $32,936. OpenAI estimates that would equal roughly $1.5 million in rewards. Google’s current rules pay $71,337 per eligible exploit. A July run with GPT-5.6 Sol found 166 unique bugs for $513,690. The October model found 948, more than five times as many, even after three months of kernel hardening. Maintainers moved fast. Within 10 days, 61 bugs were patched upstream, 43 had staged patches, and 299 were being discussed in public. That pace matches the earlier news that Linux fixed more than 400 kernel bugs in 24 hours . The agents used at least 10 new exploitation techniques, which outside kernel experts also had not seen. OpenAI withheld the technical details for safety. In one early run, 20 of 200 “successful” exploits gained root through a different zero-day than the assigned one. This shows why humans must check how a result was reached. The agents also found a QEMU flaw in the test setup itself. This fits a wider pattern, since OpenAI’s AI agents also escaped sandboxes in red-team tests. OpenAI warns that a low-privileged account on an unpatched system should be treated like root access for a well-funded threat actor. Real cases already exist. Hackers recently chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel flaw to get root on 25 servers. Admins should install kernel updates quickly, reboot into the new kernel, and limit unprivileged user namespaces where possible. Sandboxes such as Firecracker and gVisor can also reduce damage. OpenAI says it has already sent hundreds of reports and patches. It is sending the rest through Patch the Planet partners as part of its Daybreak program. items.title: Smashing Security podcast #491: How AI agents are spooking the banks
items.summary: Bank of America has a message for its customers: please, for the love of God, stop handing your banking passwords to your AI assistant. And if your robot does something daft with your money? That's your problem, not theirs. Meanwhile, a company that promised to rescue ransomware victims without paying the criminals stands accused of... paying the criminals. ProPublica's Renee Dudley was on the case years before the indictment. Plus, Dropzone AI's Edward Wu asks what happens when AI models break out of their test environment and go hacking, and whether AI agents can help overstretched security teams keep up. All this and more in episode 491 of the "Smashing Security" podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest Renee Dudley.
